theme_scores.justification: DCLG's own market research (method described: 50 agents, website search) plus EHS 2014/15, NALS, Generation Rent and Shelter figures (Refs 3,4,5,6,10) are cited and compared, and the document itself flags the resulting inconsistency ('Generation Rent's findings also demonstrate the inconsistency in fees charged'), so contradictory figures are acknowledged.

The NLA Q4 2016 survey finding that a quarter of landlords did not know if tenant fees were charged (Ref 11) is cited and linked to the claim, but the OFT 2013 study is only named in prose with no reference, and no assessment of evidence quality is offered.

theme_scores.theme: Existing transparency regulation has not worked
theme_scores.justification: The 2016 Client Money Protection call for evidence describes who was asked and what, but gives only qualitative results ('majority', 'many', 'a number') with no numbers or citation; the claim is bolstered by the cited 12% non-display figure (Ref 10) carried over from the fees theme.

theme_scores.theme: Financial harm and barriers to mobility
theme_scores.justification: Citizens' Advice's 64%/42% figures on payment problems and borrowing are properly cited (Reference 13) and directly linked to the financial-harm claim, though the EHS 35%/34% mobility stats appear here without their own citation marker.

reasoning: The diagnosis rests on four core themes. 'High and opaque tenant fees' is the strongest: DCLG's own described market research (50 agents, website search) sits alongside cited EHS, NALS, Generation Rent and Shelter data (Refs 3-6,10), and the document explicitly notes the resulting inconsistency between sources (e.g. £172 vs £223 vs £400 average fees), reaching level 3. 'Market failure from misaligned incentives' reaches level 2 via the cited NLA survey (Ref 11, 'a quarter of landlords... did not know') but the OFT 2013 study is named without citation, and no uncertainty is discussed. 'Existing transparency regulation has not worked' draws on the department's own 2016 call for evidence, which names who was asked but gives only vague quantifiers ('majority', 'many'), reaching level 2 when combined with the cited 12% non-display figure (Ref 10) reused from elsewhere. 'Financial harm and barriers to mobility' reaches level 2 through Citizens Advice's cited 64%/42% figures (Ref 13), though the EHS mobility stats lack a reference marker here. Mean of (3,2,2,2)=2.25, rounding to 2. The strongest counter-example is the uncited EHS mobility statistic and the OFT study, which show gaps in citation discipline. To reach level 3 overall, the document would need to assess the reliability or limitations of the NLA, OFT and consultation evidence, not just report their findings.
